title: Notes of Ministry - 20 - July 1974

source.file: Various/Notes of Ministry - 20 - July 1974 (2404)/Notes of Ministry - 20 - July 1 - Various.epub

paragraphs.text: It might be thought by some that what has engaged us during these two days has been on a somewhat high level, and beyond them. Therefore I have read from the epistle to the Romans, because the very holy matters we were speaking about have their elements in this epistle.
Romans is the basic epistle. It sets out the gospel according to Paul, the gospel of God concerning His Son, Jesus Christ our Lord.

The epistle begins with men, just as they are in this world, in dark heathendom, the moralists and philosophers, and the favoured Jewish nation, and condemns them all—“All have sinned, and come short of the glory of God”, Romans 3: 23. According to Romans every man, no matter what his upbringing, or his natural ability, has sinned, and the gospel introduces one Man, Jesus Christ. Chapter 5 speaks of “the one Man, Jesus Christ” (Romans 5: 15), and God in the gospel would attract every one of us to Him. This epistle is meant to set every believer in relation to the one Man, Jesus Christ. This is basic, and very important. This is where we start. Is every one here related to the one Man, Jesus Christ? How important this is! If we are going to understand anything of God’s things, we have to be related in faith and affection to the one Man, Jesus Christ.
Romans tells us how we arrive at it, “through faith in his blood” (Romans 3: 25);
faith in the blood of Jesus; how simple it is! It speaks of “him that is of the faith of Jesus”

(Romans 3: 26), very simple, very attractive: I trust everyone here has faith in the blood, and that everyone is of the faith of Jesus. It speaks about “believing on Him who has raised from among the dead Jesus our Lord, who has been delivered for our offences and has been raised for our justification”, Romans 4: 24–25. It is good to begin at the beginning, so that we are not talking over the heads of anyone, and Romans deals with all this.

Then it speaks about the believer being justified by faith—“Therefore having been justified on the principle of faith”, Romans 5: 1. We are not justified publicly. You cannot prove to any man in the world that you are a forgiven sinner. He would not require proof that you are a sinner, but you could not prove to anyone you are a forgiven sinner. The proof will come in the world to come; there will be ample evidence then. Meantime, we are justified by faith. It is a kind of secret we have, because of being related to the one Man, Jesus Christ; we are justified on the principle of faith, and have peace towards God through our Lord Jesus Christ.
These are wonderful statements, but these blessings come to us as we are in relation to the one Man, Jesus Christ.

Then it speaks in chapter 6, about freedom from sin. Twice it says, “having got your freedom from sin”, Romans 6: 18, 22. What does that mean? It means that sin is no longer your master. You have changed your master; you have changed from sin to the one Man, Jesus Christ. We were speaking about thy young man of Egypt whom David’s men found in the field, 1 Samuel 30: 13. He had served his Amalekite master, and he fell sick and his master cast him aside; he had no more use for him. David’s men found him and brought him to David, and he is fed, refreshed, and revived. He made one stipulation—‘Do not send me back to my master’. He is typical of one who is related to the one Man, Jesus Christ, and who has found all he needs in Him, and who finds fellowship and life among those who are committed to the one Man, Jesus Christ. He has got his freedom from sin, freedom from the Amalekite master, and has committed himself to another Master. Sin is for him no longer the master. Have we all got as far as this in our souls? Sin in Romans 6 is a system of things; it is all around us in the world, and Satan would have us serving sin; but let us change our master for the one Man, Jesus Christ.

In chapter 7 we read that we are “to be to another”. This involves affection, a link in affection. It has in mind not only service, but supply. It involves being nourished in affection by another. You now have another Husband: You have another Master in chapter 6, you have another Husband in chapter 7.
Chapter 8 depicts the wealth that comes to the believer in the Spirit, the Holy Spirit of God.

Romans goes over this ground, and I am going over it briefly to indicate what is available to the believer down here. It speaks about the Spirit of God dwelling in us. What do we know about this? Have you received the Spirit? Is the Spirit of God dwelling in you? We can make no progress in the things of God until we have the Spirit of God dwelling in us. Then it speaks of having the Spirit of Christ. That involves some formation; it means that the Spirit of God finds suitable dwelling conditions in the believer so that there is a formation in the Spirit of Christ.

It goes on to say that “we more than conquer through Him that has loved us”, Romans 8: 37. Think of that—not only conquer but more than conquer. Now, is that your experience? We may not be able to say much about this, but we are to know a little about it. I trust everyone here knows a little about these things. Then, just in case anyone wonders about God’s committal to the nation of Israel, Paul gives us three chapters to set every mind at rest as to God’s dealing with the nation, so that up to the end of chapter 11 every matter is set out plainly, every problem is solved as far as God is concerned and as far as the believer is concerned.
Then we have chapter 12, “I beseech you therefore, brethren, by the compassions of God, to present your bodies a living sacrifice”. Now this is something that happens from our side.

The “compassions of God” is the unfolding of God’s mercy, God’s provision. How ample, how magnanimous, it is! And then Paul exhorts them “to present your bodies …” Would you like to know anything about forming part of the one body? Would you like to know what it is to be in the family of God in reality, to form part of that divine family? Would you like to know what it is to come under divine teaching, and have a part in the care of God’s interests down here? How do you start? You begin by presenting your body a living sacrifice. There is no other way, dear brethren. Have we all done that?
Somebody here might say, ‘I do not get all the help from the Spirit that I would like to get’.

Have you ever presented your body a living sacrifice? Maybe the Spirit is waiting for you until this presentation comes from your side. The Spirit will not present your body for you; it is what you do, what each one of us does; “… present your bodies a living sacrifice”. This means that your body, the members of your body, the faculties you have, you commit, you hand over, to God without recall. Have you ever done that? Dear brother or sister, you can do it now. Do not wait until you get home; do it now!

You can confirm it when you get home, but do it now. If you feel any urge, if you have any sense of God’s compassions and God’s provision, if you feel any desires within you to come into the good of what we have been speaking about these two days, then, I would say to you,

‘Present your body a living sacrifice, holy, acceptable to God’. You say, ‘Will God accept my body?’ Yes, it is acceptable to God. It may be that the Spirit is waiting until someone here presents his body, or her body, and then He will say, ‘Now I can help you; now I can provide you far more supply than ever you have known in the past’. Any deficiency with us in knowing the help of the Spirit and the wealth of divine provision could be traced to a lack of committal of this kind.
This is the beginning of discipleship. This is how the believer becomes a disciple. The moment comes when he presents his body a living sacrifice. He may not always live up to it;

maybe no one here could say that he has always lived up to his committal, but do not let us be shaken in our committal; let any failure we have had reconfirm our committal that our body is presented “holy, acceptable to God, which is your intelligent service”. This word for “service” is priestly service, it is a priestly action; it is presenting to God something acceptable. Think of that! This is possible for every one of us. This is how we begin to come into the wealth of the things of God, and there is no means of coming into the wealth of what God has for us apart from the presentation of our

bodies. Thus we become disciples. We become committed to the will of God, as it says, “Be not conformed to this world, but be transformed by the renewing of your mind, that ye may prove what is the good and acceptable and perfect will of God”.

Think of persons down here whose bodies are committed to the will of God: What a privilege we have, what a privilege everyone here has! Would someone say, ‘I would rather have my own way; I would rather have things as I want them; I would rather have my own natural inclinations satisfied; I would rather be in a circle where things are according to what pleases me’? That is not presenting your body a living sacrifice, and that is not proving what is the good and acceptable and perfect will of God. The gospel tells you the will of God is good.

There is nothing better for you than to commit yourself to the will of God. It is acceptable. As you accept the glad tidings as to the goodness of the will of God, you find it acceptable; then you prove it to be perfect. It is far better than your own way, or your own natural inclinations or your own natural tastes. It is the perfect will of God.

It goes on, “For I say, through the grace which has been given to me, to every one that is among you, not to have high thoughts above what he should think; but to think so as to be wise, as God has dealt to each a measure of faith”. Have you a measure of faith? Has each one here found what his measure of faith is? I believe you will never know what your measure of faith is until you present your body a living sacrifice. You have a measure, a part to fill, according to the will of God. So you do not have high thoughts above what you should think, but you have something. I remember Mr. E. T. Maynard saying, to illustrate

what we are speaking about: ‘If I have a pound and I say I have two pounds, I am not right; but if I have a pound and say I have nothing, I am not right either’. If I have a pound I have something. Thus you find you have a measure of faith and you function according to the measure of faith God has sovereignly given.

Paul then goes on to speak about the one body as “one body in Christ”; not in Adam, not in human organisation, but “one body in Christ”. By presenting your body a living sacrifice to God, and by being with persons locally, you find what your measure of faith is, and then you begin to find your place in the body. Mr. Stoney used to emphasise the importance of finding our place in the body. There is a place and function in this wonderful organism down here. It speaks of “a measure of faith” in verse 3, and in verse 6 of “the proportion of faith”, and “the grace which has been given to us”. There is a measure and proportion of faith and grace to fill out our place in the body. This is not difficult to understand. You present your body a living sacrifice, you think of yourself soberly, locally, and you find you have a measure of faith, and grace which has been given, and you thus function in the one body in Christ.

The one body in Christ is universal; it is the one body down here at any given moment. There was one body in Christ on the earth when Paul wrote this, and there is one body in Christ on the earth at this moment; and by presenting my body a living sacrifice I find, in some sense, what it is to have a measure and proportion, and the gift of grace, that help me to function in the one body in Christ. It is a wonderful order of things. This shows the way into it simply, not beyond the reach of any believer.

It goes on, “Thus we, being many, are one body in Christ, and each one members one of the other”; it is an organism down here where believers belong to one another, and form one body in Christ—that is its status and it is animated by the Spirit of Christ. It is a wonderful order of things down here into which believers are called by the gospel to have part in functionally at this moment. Although there is public breakdown and public confusion, this is meant actually to function down here.

So Paul goes on to speak about “members one of the other”. You will notice in the scriptures read that this expression “one another” comes in. The one body in Christ is universal; it is the one body down here; yet things are meant to function locally, and we have regard to one another; we are members one of another. According to 1 Corinthians 6, our bodies are members of Christ. “Do ye not know that your bodies are members of Christ?”, 1 Corinthinas 6: 15. Think of that! Your body, presented to God a living sacrifice, becomes a member of Christ, a member for the expression of Christ. It is a wonderful possibility for each one of us to enter into by way of committal.

It speaks about various services, different gifts; there is great variety, but as we function according to our measure of faith, according to the proportion we have, there is no collision, the variety all fits in. It speaks in Peter about “the various grace of God” (1 Peter 4: 10), something given to one, something else to another, and all functions normally and smoothly; that is the divine idea. You come into it by presenting your body a living sacrifice, and there is no other way. Paul says, “as to brotherly love, kindly affectioned towards one another—as to honour, each taking the lead in paying it to the other”. It comes down to two persons, the one to the other; and no matter how many more there are, this principle operates, it is one another. It is the family also; it is one another as belonging to that family.

Chapter 14 says, “So then let us pursue the things which tend to peace”. We were speaking about using diligence to keep the unity of the Spirit in the uniting bond of peace. You find the element of that here—“Let us pursue the things which tend to peace”. Can we all commit ourselves to that, as having presented our bodies a living sacrifice, in order to fulfil the will of God? Then let us pursue the things which tend to peace. Then it says, “And things whereby one shall build up another”. There are the things of peace and the things of mutual

edification. So there is an order of things that is being built up. We touched in Ephesians on the body in its fulness, in its self-building up in love (Ephesians 4: 16); here; each one has a part in that building up and mutual edification.

In chapter 15 we have, “The God of endurance and of encouragement give to you to be like-minded one toward another, according to Christ Jesus”. This does not mean that all the brethren have to come round to what I think! Someone said, ‘It would save an awful lot of trouble if everybody just thought the way I think’; but it says here, “according to Christ Jesus”. It is a local setting, it says, “that ye may”; “… give to you”; and “… that ye may with one accord, with one mouth, glorify the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ”; it is one answer locally to the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ.

What a possibility! It is more than a possibility, it is working; but it is a possibility for each one here to function in this one thing for the pleasure and glory of God. “Wherefore receive ye one another, according as the Christ also has received you to the glory of God”.

Then Paul says, “I am persuaded, my brethren, I myself also, concerning you, that yourselves also are full of goodness, filled with all knowledge, able also to admonish one another”. This would involve taking on care for one another, taking on responsibility for one another. “Able also to admonish one another”; there is such a family atmosphere, and such a mutuality, that there is the admonishing of one another. There is not an official admonisher in the locality; it is admonishing one another. It is how we practically help one another.

Then, finally, “Salute one another with a holy kiss”. Paul has been presenting his salutations to individuals who were in Rome. It is one thing to salute somebody at a distance, but we are sometimes tested as to whether we always salute one another with a holy kiss. We read about Joseph that the first indication of something wrong in the family was that his brethren could not greet him with friendliness. We have known something of that. Let us continue to salute one another with a holy kiss.

I remember Mr. Taylor coming to Edinburgh and giving an address on ‘A holy kiss’, and the next night he had a reading on ‘Local assembly administration’. You will find in the volume (N.S. 43) that the reading comes before the address, but actually the address came first on the need for the maintenance of

brotherly and sisterly relations locally, which would provide conditions for good administration. There is something instructive and important in that. Let us continue, dear brethren, to salute one another with a holy kiss. May it be so.

I felt led, beloved brethren, to say a word in relation to that which descends, that which has that character of descending. Naturally, as fallen creatures, we take character from what is fallen, but I believe what we are being encouraged with in these meetings is to take character from that which descends. We have been taught that what descends is illuminating, but that what falls is darkening. It is an affecting thing that two Persons of the Godhead are spoken of in this way as descending. It would affect our hearts as we think, beloved brethren, that the Lord Jesus has descended into the lower parts of the earth. He has been lower than any. Think of the grace of the Lord Jesus in that. This is in a setting of victory and of triumph, for the One who descended is the One who has ascended far above all heavens, and He has great spoil as the result of His victory. Think of the spoil the Lord has, and He is devoting that spoil toward the assembly. For these gifts, which are part of His spoil, are devoted to the assembly, for the upbuilding of the assembly, that which He

delights in, that which is to take character from Him. And the end in view, as we were reminded today, is “until we all arrive at the unity of the faith and of the knowledge of the Son of God, at the full-grown man, at the measure of the stature of the fulness of the Christ”.

Well, beloved brethren, the character of that manhood is that it descends. The impression I have is as to how it was exemplified in the apostle Paul. At Troas, in relation to Eutychus, it says he descended. The Lord Jesus is mighty in His victory, but how the glory of the moral excellence of His manhood comes out. It is not just an arbitrary matter that gives Him this place of supremacy, it is because of the moral worth and excellence that are in Him. Moral excellence is developed on this line of descent. It, is emphasised in the epistle to the Philippians as well; moral excellence was seen in that company, and in the way that the apostle Paul speaks of the mind that was in Christ Jesus, the mind to go down. How different from the mind to go up which has marked Satan and marks man as fallen. The mind to go up takes character from what is fallen—but how beautiful it is to see that which takes character from Christ in this way, that which descends.

Then, too, we have been speaking of the lowly place the Holy Spirit has taken. I have been affected by that. Really, if we move in the grace which was seen in Christ, if that feature is to be seen with us, it can only be as we are committed to the Holy Spirit and He takes charge of us.
We know from the good teaching that the baptism of the Lord Jesus was when the economy came on to view for the first time.

What a marvellous dispensation we are in, beloved brethren, when God has revealed Himself in this way in the economy, as we speak of it, this wondrous economy of love; and God has a part for us in this economy, a part for men. We have been called to the greatest things. Oh, beloved brethren, think of the greatness of divine things, the greatness of the way that God has come out to secure our affections, to secure our confidence and to secure our trust in every way. It says that “the Holy Spirit descended in a bodily form as a dove” upon Jesus. In all those movements of grace seen in the Lord Jesus He moved in the power of the Holy Spirit. He says to His disciples in John 14: 17, concerning the Spirit, “Ye know him”. What wonderful grace there was about the Lord Jesus in His movements; and the Spirit was with Him in those movements. The Spirit descended in a bodily form as a dove upon Him, pointing out, I believe, the lowly place the Spirit has taken in this wondrous economy. What lowliness marks the blessed Spirit of God! We think with reverence of the glory and greatness of His Person, of who He is, One with the Father and the Son. How it behoves us to be reverent in the presence of the Spirit of God. But how lowly He is, and how He delighted fully to identify Himself with the Lord Jesus. Then there is the voice out of heaven, “Thou art my beloved Son, in thee I have found my delight”.
I desired just to point out, beloved brethren, the place the Spirit has taken; the way that He has come, too, to take His abode in the assembly, the way He came at Pentecost—what a descent that was!

So I believe that the grace in which the assembly moves shows the way in which she takes character from Christ, and takes character from the Holy Spirit. John says in Revelation 21, “I saw the holy city, new Jerusalem, coming down out of the heaven from God”. She comes from God, descending out of heaven, illuminating everything. What a wonderful thing it is to have part in this glorious vessel. We are being formed now for our place eternally in this city, the city which has this character. It does not say that she came down, it is “coming down”, as if it is a characteristic feature with her. We are being formed to have part in this wondrous vessel now.

I feel my limitations in speaking of it, but it is what marks this glorious dispensation. It has marked divine Persons Themselves that they have descended, and it marks the holy city, new Jerusalem. What a wonderful thing it is, beloved brethren, to take character from divine Persons. We have been speaking about taking character from God, as being His children. The Lord Jesus has set things out in perfection, and then also we can learn the blessed features of the Holy Spirit through the manhood of Jesus.

May we grow in acquaintance with the Lord Jesus. What depths there are to learn in the knowledge of Him, the knowledge of the Holy Spirit, and the knowledge of the Father. May we be helped in it, for His name’s sake.

Our brother has referred to the divine economy coming to light in the descent of the Holy Spirit upon Jesus. What an economy that is to contemplate, beloved brethren, the operations of the Trinity. What riches of wisdom, what divine resources, have entered into it, that God should thus be known; Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. And, as our brother has remarked, two divine Persons have descended. What operations were effected in that economy in the manhood of Jesus—and what operations are continuing now; the Lord Jesus no longer here, but the assembly being here.

This scripture would draw attention to what operated in a local assembly. We have had a good deal in these meetings bearing on us in our localities, where these operations and exercises take practical shape; where we learn most of our lessons; where we face exercises, where we are tested most, and where, I think—because that is where we spend most of our lives—we profit most, though we are deeply thankful for such occasions as these in which we can all be under the Lord’s teaching together, and return to our localities stimulated, encouraged, and enlightened as to what is being worked out in this dispensation, that in every place there might be what is Pauline, what Paul would ordain in all the assemblies.

Antioch represents something of very great distinction in local conditions. There were men there who had come under the formative influence of the Lord Jesus, and the Spirit was free to be in relation to them. How ready the Holy Spirit would ever be to identify Himself with what in character and moral formation is akin to Christ.

So that, first of all, we have what was in a city, “there were in Antioch …” How great heaven’s interest is in every place from which we come. This would encourage us, that heaven has its eye on places. We have had a good many suggestions today as to our outlook upon all who belong to the Lord. Many of them are not claiming that which belongs to them, but we would hold it for them and desire that there might be such conditions among us that the Lord may be free to work in recovery.

But not only is there the place, the city, but it says, “there were in Antioch, in the assembly which was there”. What was specifically under heaven’s eye was that which was marked by the true features of the assembly, to be seen later coming down out of heaven, but seen in the spirit of that in Antioch. I think as we look upon one another today we have a fresh sense of the preciousness of what is of assembly character in many places, which is to be cherished, nurtured, and protected. These persons were “in the assembly”. I think the Lord would ask us whether we are “in the assembly”; whether above everything else with which we have to do, and above every other circle in which we righteously move, we regard ourselves as in the assembly; not on the fringe of it, not spectators as to it, but, if I may say so, immersed in it. In
our affections and our exercises, in any service, and in our prayers, we are to be in the assembly. Is not Christ wholly related to it? He loved the assembly,

and delivered Himself up for it. Let us not in any sense bring in any element of friction, or of the Esau line, but rather use diligence, as we have been reminded, “to keep the unity of the Spirit in the uniting bond of peace”, Ephesians 4: 3.

Certain persons are named here. We might well think that Antioch was a very favoured locality to have such men in it, but, dear brethren, how thankful we should be for those whom the Lord has given us to walk with. As was remarked earlier, He has chosen our brethren; we have not chosen them; and He has chosen the best for us so that the working out of the economy might proceed according to divine wisdom in the places in which we have been set.

The carnal mind, looking over this list of very diverse persons, including possibly a coloured man, an aristocrat, the foster brother of Herod, and outstanding men like Saul and Barnabas, might say, ‘However will all these persons get on together? There will be rivalry, there will be place-seeking’. But not at all, because the descending line was being maintained. It says they were “ministering to the Lord and fasting”. That was the descending line, the mind which was in Christ Jesus. Dear brethren, we shall cease to be of help in our localities if we are not maintained on the line of fasting, the negation of the mind to go up, that would seek prominence. These men were fasting; they were continually hard on the flesh; they were keeping the feast of unleavened bread, and they were ministering to the Lord.

These two lines indeed go on together, the descending line and the ascending line. No doubt the service of God in Antioch was something extremely fine and rich as they ministered to the Lord in their comings together.

And what this leads to is the liberty of the Holy Spirit to link Himself on with such persons in such an atmosphere. There was clearly a family atmosphere in Antioch. This has been much before us happy, mutual, family conditions, and yet there was what was distinctive in personality, as it says, “prophets and teachers”. We may not have this in outstanding form, but, dear brethren, where there is love and desire these things will work out and come into evidence. We are to desire to prophesy (1 Corinthians 14: 1), and I feel it is one of our greatest needs in some of our places that there should be the fervent desire simply to be available to the Lord to bring in His mind. The Lord is wanting, and the Spirit is seeking, suitable vessels through whom the abundance of heaven can be channelled prophetically and livingly into the local assembly. There is also the constant need of teaching. There may not be much gift, but the Lord would help, and the Spirit would strengthen those who are devoted to the truth, so that the purity and the clarity of the truth should be preserved in our localities.

So the Spirit was free in. Antioch. If I may connect it with the scripture our brother read in Luke 3 (which, of course, is distinct and unique, the Spirit identifying Himself with Jesus) the Spirit was free and unhindered to identify Himself with the conditions and the persons in Antioch. He says, “Separate me now …” as if the setting was so pleasing to Him that He takes over certain persons for wider work.

This is like what we had earlier as to what works out in one generation and then in another; what was there in Jacob and what there was in all its attractiveness and fulness in Joseph. I would appeal to the beloved younger people here. The Spirit is intensely interested in you. Those of us who are older should have a special sense of the way in which the Spirit in His infinite patience has been with us. He has surrendered nothing when we were prepared to surrender many things. His faithfulness is one of the most affecting contemplations. And now, I think, He would give us a sense of how ready He is to use available vessels, that the great workings of the economy, the operations of God and of Christ in the assembly, might continue in His own power and in His own grace.
So He says, “Separate me now Barnabas and Saul for the work to which I have called them”.

Let us be in the hands of the Spirit. Let us not aspire to do great things, but let us fervently desire to be available for what needs to be done, however simple it may be, and the simpler we are, dear brethren, in one way, the better. Let us be simple in our committal to the saints and do what needs to be done selflessly in love for Christ and love for the brethren.

We see the family feature working out here—“Having fasted and prayed, and having laid their hands on them, they let them go”. How much flowed out of this city of Antioch in influence. Pauline influence above all, and I do not doubt that the Spirit would develop in every locality what will be influential for good beyond its own borders. Paul loved to speak of the saints in certain localities. They were his boast; he loved to speak of the work of God, and I think this is a very precious feature, that what is secured in any one place has an influence

far beyond its borders. That was certainly the case in Antioch. There were such conditions there that the Spirit said, as it were, ‘I will take over these persons so that what has been formed in this city shall now be extended to the benefit of the saints in a much wider way’.

May we be encouraged. Maybe we are in smallness in our localities, but think of the character and the preciousness of what is there, and that what is proceeding is essentially and directly related to the great divine operations in this dispensation. May God bless this to us.

I had an impression, beloved brethren, to refer to this section of Scripture because of the references to not being ashamed. Paul says, “Be not therefore ashamed of the testimony of our Lord, nor of me his prisoner”. Then he says in verse 12, “I am not ashamed”. And Onesiphorus was not ashamed of Paul’s chain. On the other hand, Phygellus and Hermogenes and all in Asia clearly were ashamed of Paul.
We have been speaking today of the truth as to Christ and the assembly; the glory of the body of Christ. And what is the body of Christ for but the display of Himself? We

have been reminded of Revelation 21, when the city will be for the display of God in all His greatness, and of the assembly being the fulness of Him who fills all in all; but the assembly is to be for the display of Christ even now. One has felt challenged in recent times as to the importance of being found in the testimony, and among those where Christ is seen in display.

Paul says here, “Be not therefore ashamed of the testimony of our Lord”. Do you ever feel ashamed of the testimony? You may say, ‘Well, yes, when people talk about publicly-known failure in recent times’. I believe, beloved brethren, that in a day like this there is a special demand to be found faithful in the testimony.
There has been a history of much failure, in which we have each had our part, but that is not to cause us to be ashamed of the testimony of our Lord. Let me ask you a simple question.

When did you last confess the name of the Lord Jesus to a person other than amongst your brethren? Is it so long ago that you cannot remember? It is of vital importance to be in the testimony in faithfulness to Christ, for our present salvation depends to a large degree on our preparedness to be found thus. In a day when things have gone to wrack and ruin publicly, what need there is that you and I should stand in the breach as never before and be faithful to the name of the Lord Jesus. So Paul would encourage us—“Be not therefore ashamed of the testimony of our Lord”. What an encouragement to us to be found in the testimony of our Lord Jesus! The Lord is in disrepute; the name of the Lord is, alas, not welcomed in the world. It brings, reproach, and who of us likes reproach? When we speak of reproach we think of Moses. He took the long-term view; he was not ashamed
of the reproach of Christ, then think of his reward!
Then Paul adds, “nor of me his prisoner”. Now Paul is in disrepute as well, but there is encouragement not only not to be ashamed of Christ, but not to be ashamed of Paul either.
The truth as to Christ and the assembly, the light which has come to us at its height, is not popular. Alas, how few comparatively there are here today; how few there are as you look

round generally; this but testifies to the fact that Paul is in reproach. How thankful we can be for the truth which has come to us, the light to which we have been recovered as to the Head in heaven and the body here on earth. That was Paul’s distinctive ministry. How thankful we can be for the ministries, the outline of sound words, which have unfolded the truth to us. We need to value and to read the ministry so as to “have an outline of sound words, which words thou hast heard of me, in faith and love which are in Christ Jesus”. It is not to be something which we read and take in in an intellectual way, but it is to be kept “by the Holy Spirit which dwells in us”; then it will not be just knowledge, it will be worked out in a substantial character. Thus there will be this testimony as to Christ, and a representation concretely of the truth as to the assembly.

What an example Paul himself is to us. He says, “I am not ashamed”. In days when there were such persons as Phygellus around, and all in Asia had turned away from Paul you might think he would have been very despondent. Is Paul ashamed, because of what had come in to mar the testimony, to spoil the features of Christ in the saints, for which he had laboured? No,
“I am not ashamed”. Why?

“For I know whom I have believed”. He had a link with the Man in the glory. He does not say I know what I have believed, but “whom I have believed”. Paul was almost on his own, and you feel very much for those now who are just two or three, but in such circumstances Paul was not ashamed. He was as bright as ever, as buoyant as ever; “I am not ashamed; for I know whom I have believed, and am persuaded that he is able to keep for that day the deposit I have entrusted to him”. Now where is your deposit? Paul’s deposit was not in a bank here, it was with Christ in glory. He had Christ as his Object, and, come what may, you could not have deflected Paul. Christ had met him on the Damascus road, he had seen Christ in glory, and that was what was governing him in his pathway here. So, though things outwardly are weak and there is much to sorrow over, Paul would encourage us to go on, and to prove the power of Christ on high, and the Spirit here below, to support and encourage us in the testimony.

Then Paul says, “All who are in Asia … have turned away from me”. It does not say that they had turned away from the Lord; they had not necessarily turned away, you might say, from an evangelical line; but they had turned away from Paul and Paul’s glad tidings, the truth at its height. Because the Spirit is here, there will be what is collective to the end. How thankful we can be for that! That is involved in Paul’s glad tidings. Those who turned away from Paul gave up the truth as to the assembly. We can say that, objectively, every believer having the Spirit is in the assembly; but the Spirit’s great work is that the truth should not just be objective, but should be worked out substantially, and that we, as in the circle where the truth is worked out collectively, should be there not just as
being right positionally, but as fitted together in a substantial way. We are not to be isolated individual units, but built together, fitted together, to be a habitation of God in Spirit.
How sad that some have given up the truth as to what is collective and go on as if they were isolated individual units. May we continue as those who are built up together and maintained

together in the truth at its height as to Christ and the assembly. We shall not then be found among those of whom Paul says, “All who are in Asia, of whom is Phygellus and Hermogenes, have turned away from me”. We would be among those who go on and seek in faithfulness to maintain what has been committed to us. How full is the light that has been committed to us! What a responsibility is upon us; but what encouragement to be found as those who are livingly and vitally in the testimony, personally, householdly, and collectively.

Then there is this man, Onesiphorus, and his household. He was not ashamed of Paul, or of Paul’s chain. It would have taken courage to go and visit that Roman jail where Paul was a prisoner. He would have been immediately identified with Paul. Would you like to be identified with a prisoner like Paul? It would test us. Onesiphorus sought out Paul very diligently and refreshed him. What an encouragement to Paul! “The Lord grant to him to find mercy from the Lord in that day—and how much service he rendered in Ephesus thou knowest best”.
So what encouragement there is, beloved brethren, that we should be found as those who are not ashamed. We have much entrusted

to us—all the light that has shone out, which we have here in the Scriptures, made good to us in the power of the Spirit; all that has been opened up to our understanding through the ministry that has come to us how thankful we can be! But I believe the call of the day is for persons who are faithful, standing in the testimony, and not ashamed of Christ, not ashamed of Paul’s glad tidings, and not ashamed of Paul’s chain.

May we all be encouraged, even though we be in days of weakness and brokenness, to be found as those who would continue, with the Lord’s help and that of the Holy Spirit, to seek to hold the truth at its height, not having any lower standard. That would test us in our individual pathways, but what a comfort to the heart of the Lord that there should be little companies on the face of this earth in which He has been rejected, who accept His rejection, and who seek to be faithful to Him in the little time that remains until we shall be with Him for ever.
